newsitem.title: USA: U.S. blue chips rally on relief over wage data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blue chips rally on relief over wage data.

text.p: U.S. blue chips scrambled higher on Friday as Wall Street breathed a collective sigh of relief after the release of a key monthly jobs report.
The Dow industrials jumped 56 points to close unofficially at 7001, after spending much of the session comfortably above the milestone level.

But a week's worth of wear and tear clearly showed at the end of the session, as stocks appeared exhausted by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's seemingly countless speaking appearances and the jitters of waiting for the jobs report.
At every turn, it seemed, investors were preparing for one event that would settle definitively the near term outlook for interest rates and inflation.

"You had people coming in expecting the world to end when Greenspan spoke," said Dick Stein, vice president at U.S. Clearing Corp. "When it didn't, they came in again today expecting the world to end."
Instead, markets dodged a bullet because the February payrolls report included figures that initially appeared to realize some of Wall Street's worst fears.
The data showed 339,000 new non-farm jobs were created in February, far outstripping forecasts, which averaged 230,000.

However, despite the booming jobs market, wage growth remained tame, with average hourly wages rising a less than expected 0.2 percent. The nation's unemployment rate edged down to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent, in line with forecasts.

The mixed message sparked life into the market, which had girded for the worst, but the ensuing rally seemed to lack the market's hallmark confidence of old, as blue chips barely clawed their way to 7000 and techs sputtered to losses.

"Today was nothing more than relief and this was a rather weakened looking rally," said Richard Cripps chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "Before, stocks always wanted to find a way to go up. Lately, Nasdaq has been looking for a reason to go down."
Analysts said even with the jobs report over, the market was still seeking direction and might not find it for weeks.

"On balance the bias seems to have an uptilt," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock and Co. "But it appears the market is likely to trade in a tight range ahead of the Fed's next meeting (on March 25)."

The rally brought the Dow's gains for the week to about 123 points and powered the average to its first close over 7000 since February 25, the session preceding the first of Greenspan's two Humphrey-Hawkins addresses to Congress.
Financial stocks had a strong day, aided by a bond market rally that drove the yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury down to 6.82 percent from 6.88 percent.
Citicorp rose 3-1/4 to 125-3/4, Chase Manhattan Corp gained 3-3/4 to 106-1/2 and BankAmerica Corp climbed 3-1/4 to 122.

Technology stocks were weak, as several issues met with stiff selling. Atmel Corp fell 4-3/4 to 26-3/4 after saying its fiscal first quarter results would fall short of estimates. Atmel's woes also dragged down rival Microchip Technology Inc, which lost 6-5/16 to 29-1/4.
The broad selling pressure extended even to the top tier of tech names. Intel Corp fell 1-7/8 to 143-1/2 and Microsoft Corp shed one to 96-3/4.
Texas Instruments Inc bucked the trend, rising 3-3/8 to 83-7/8 after Merrill Lynch raised its long-term rating on the shares to buy from accumulate.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 3.63 points to 1311.80.
The S&P 500 index rose 6.41 points to 804.97.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
